title: ExxonMobil’s Refining Profits Are Set to Jump $4.5 Billion. Here’s What XOM Investors Need to Know. - The Motley Fool
content: Exxon is benefiting from having an integrated business. ExxonMobil (XOM +2.46%) just gave investors an initial glimpse at its upcoming third-quarter earnings report. The oil giant noted that it expects strong refining margins to add $4.5 billion to its earnings in the period. That's more than double the earnings from its energy products segment in the second quarter. However, there were some offsetting headwinds elsewhere across its portfolio that will mute some of that positive impact. Here's everything ExxonMobil investors need to know about its preliminary third-quarter earnings update. ExxonMobil typically provides investors with an initial glimpse of its upcoming earnings report a couple of weeks before its scheduled release (Oct. 30 for the third quarter of 2026). That gives analysts and investors a heads-up on any potential meaningful impacts during the quarter. The biggest thing that jumps out in its preliminary third-quarter numbers is the impact that changes in refining margins had on earnings from its energy products segment. Exxon reported a $4.5 billion positive effect in the third quarter. While the company noted that external impacts on its operations will shave $400 million from that total, changes in scheduled maintenance and the benefit of having more days in the third quarter will offset most of that headwind ($300 million positive impact). As a result, Exxon expects its energy products segment's earnings to more than double compared to the second quarter ($4.1 billion). However, the positive impact of strong refining margins was one of the many moving parts for Exxon in the second quarter. The company battled additional headwinds (lower liquids prices, external impacts, and timing issues) while benefiting from tailwinds (higher natural gas prices and the positive impact of some divestments). The net effect is that Exxon expects to report about $15.1 billion of adjusted earnings in the third quarter, up from $14.7 billion in the second quarter. ExxonMobil is one of several large integrated energy companies, which means it has upstream oil and gas exploration and production operations, midstream logistics assets, and a downstream business (refining and chemicals). Its stock price has already more than doubled this year due to strong refining margins. Meanwhile, Phillips 66 has increased its dividend every year since the 2012 spinoff, growing it at a 14% compound annual rate. title: Why Are BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX, USO, UCO Stocks Rising Overnight? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of multiple oil companies and oil exchange-traded funds climbed overnight late Sunday after Brent crude prices rose above $90 a barrel amid escalating tensions between the U.S. and Iran. Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, noted on X late Sunday, “Responding to this weekend's US-Iran escalation, Brent crude is currently above $90 a barrel in Asian trading.” WTI crude futures expiring in August also rose more than 2% to $84.33 per barrel. As a result, oil companies Battalion Oil Corp. (BATL) and Trio Petroleum Corp. (TPET) rose more than 7% and by over 8% in the overnight session. Oil majors Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and Chevron Corp. (CVX) also rose about 1% each. Meanwhile, the United States Oil Fund (USO), which tracks the daily price movements of West Texas Intermediate (WTI), climbed more than 2% at the time of writing, while ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil (UCO) rallied more than 3%. The Light, Sweet Crude Oil Futures (CL_F) were also 2% higher. Oil prices soared back up as tensions between the U.S. and Iran escalated over the weekend after the American military launched a ninth consecutive night of attacks on the Middle Eastern country. “CENTCOM began conducting a new wave of strikes against Iran at 7 p.m. ET today for the ninth consecutive night. The strikes will continue degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” the U.S. Central Command said in a post on X. Over the weekend, CENTCOM confirmed that a third U.S. service member had died following recent fighting in the Middle East. The military had initially reported two fatalities and one service member missing after an Iranian attack in Jordan on July 17 before later confirming the third death. Meanwhile, Iran Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi condemned the U.S. strike on the under-construction Darquoin power plant, calling it a dangerous attack on Iran's civilian infrastructure. In a post on X, he said the strike made Washington fully responsible for the resulting instability and warned that Iran would take appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and interests. "The longer the Strait remains closed and the war escalates the greater ​the risk that oil prices will have to rise to around $150/barrel to bring demand down to match the hit to supply," Shane Oliver, Head of Investment Strategy and Chief Economist, at AMP reportedly told Reuters, adding that "This is not our base case but it's a high risk again." Meanwhile, Garfield Reynolds, MLIV Asia team leader at Bloomberg, reportedly said the widening spread between Brent crude and WTI reflects growing concerns that an escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict could disrupt global energy supplies, though the gap remains narrow enough that equity markets have largely shrugged off the risk compared with the early stages of the war. Analyst Patrick De Haan said on X that rising oil prices would likely send gas prices higher in the U.S. in the coming week. “Brent crude oil up ~3% reaching $90/bbl, while WTI crude up ~2% to nearly $85/bbl. RBOB up 5c/gal, national average gas price will hit $4/gal either tomorrow or Tuesday, likely to see increases ahead for most states!” he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BATL stock slipped from ‘extremely bullish’ to ‘bullish’ over 24 hours while it was in the ‘neutral’ territory for TPET. XOM and CVX stocks were trending in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing. Sentiment for USO and UCO stocks, meanwhile, was in the ‘extremely bullish’ and ‘bearish’ territories, respectively. One bullish user on Stocktwits said, “$USO $BATL I'm not selling, no matter what." BATL stock is up more than 46% this year, while TPET has declined nearly 60% in the same time. XOM and CVX have gained more than 20% each in 2026. USO and UCO have surged nearly 80% and 113% year-to-date. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Advanced Micro Devices appears to have secured, or is close to securing, Claude developer Anthropic as a chip customer, with speculation swirling online after a senior executive referenced the AI startup in code published on GitHub. AMD shares rose 1.3% in the overnight session late Sunday. A YAML code file from an unnamed AMD senior director listed Anthropic as a “customer,” chip news site SemiAnalysis reported on Sunday. SemiAnalysis said Anthropic was assigned the maximum 30 “priority boost points,” placing it alongside existing hyperscale customers such as Meta – fueling speculation that AMD could formally announce a partnership with the AI startup at its flagship Advancing AI conference next week. “Note that Anthropic is still in the evaluation phase, and if AMD doesn’t announce Anthropic at its upcoming Advancing AI conference, that means @AnushElangovan’s FDE team has yet to address all of Anthropic’s concerns regarding software quality, and further improvement will be needed,” SemiAnalysis wrote. Meanwhile, Anthropic has reportedly been hiring engineers with ROCm experience (AMD’s AI software stack), suggesting it is preparing to further diversify its computing infrastructure, Jefferies analyst Blayne Curtis said in a recent note. Anthropic is not a publicly confirmed AMD customer. The AI startup has publicly said it trains and serves Claude using a mix of Nvidia GPUs, Amazon’s Trainium chips, and Google’s TPUs, with Amazon remaining its primary cloud and training partner. The AMD Advancing AI 2026 conference will run over Wednesday and Thursday at the Moscone Center in San Francisco. The company is expected to focus its announcements around AI infrastructure, new silicon-to-software pipelines, and enterprise-tier development. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for AMD remained ‘bullish,’ unchanged from the previous day, with traders noting speculation that Anthropic is becoming an AMD customer. “The recent market bloodbath just flushed $AMD from its 584 peak to the 490s. Daily RSI is screaming deep oversold in the 29-34 range. This is exactly what an extreme discount looks like,” a trader wrote. “The massive ‘Advancing AI’ event drops July 22-23 with the 2nm Zen 6 and Helios platform. This killer catalyst will likely torch the shorts, triggering a violent rebound off the $478 hard support next week,” they said. AMD stock has declined for three days straight, losing 16%, but remains 132% higher year to date. The chipmaker will report its second-quarter results on Aug. 4. AtaiBeckley (ATAI), Palo Alto Networks (PANW) and Travelers Companies (TRV), all reached 52-week highs on Friday as investors moved away from vulnerable areas of the technology sector and toward companies backed by stronger fundamentals, with capital flowing into businesses with clearer growth catalysts, essential services and proven earnings power. Atai Life Sciences and Palo Alto Networks stocks ended the session 0.9% and 1% higher, while Travelers Companies stock climbed 9%. AtaiBeckley stock reached a four-year high of $7.22 on Friday, as its psychedelic medicine business gained momentum after a multibillion-dollar acquisition agreement reshaped investor expectations for the sector. The rally followed Eli Lilly and Co. (LLY )'s July 16 announcement of a deal to acquire AtaiBeckley for $6.75 per share in upfront cash, valued at up to $3.8 billion, including milestone-based payments. The transaction pushed psychedelic treatments closer to mainstream pharmaceutical acceptance as investors viewed the acquisition as a sign of confidence from a major drugmaker. The deal centers on AtaiBeckley’s experimental therapies, including BPL-003 and VLS-01. BPL-003, an intranasal formulation based on 5-MeO-DMT, is being developed for treatment-resistant depression and has received FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. Palo Alto Networks stock touched a record high of $368.80 as investors showed confidence in its cybersecurity business. Demand increased for Palo Alto’s security platforms, including Cortex and XSIAM, as companies prioritized protecting their digital systems from growing AI threats. Capital One upgraded the stock to “Overweight” from “Equalweight” and increased its price target to $421 from $307. The firm expects the cybersecurity company to benefit from growing demand for AI infrastructure, rising cyber threats, a spike in security spending and the need to protect new AI systems. Retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘bearish’ territory. The Travelers Companies stock also reached a record high of $370.43 after reporting stronger-than-expected fiscal second-quarter results. The insurer posted earnings of $10.04 per share, while revenue reached $12.15 billion, both exceeding the analysts’ consensus estimates of $5.39 and $10.98 billion, respectively, according to Fiscal AI data. Travelers improved its combined ratio to 83.6% from 90.3% last year, showing stronger underwriting performance. Investor sentiment toward the stock remained positive. NFLX stock fell more than 7% at close on Friday as investors continued to react negatively to the company’s latest earnings outlook. ORCL declined to a 52-week low before reversing to close up 1.77%. SPCX stock extended two consecutive weeks of losses to close down more than 5%. NFLX stock fell to a yearly low of $65.08, about 45% down from its 12-month high, as the streaming giant’s weaker-than-expected outlook for the third quarter deepened investor concerns about its future growth. The company forecast third-quarter earnings of $0.82 per share on $12.86 billion in revenue, slightly below analysts' expectations. However, during the earnings call, CFO Spencer Neumann said quarterly growth may appear uneven due to tougher comparisons with last year, stressing that Netflix remains focused on full-year performance. He expects third-quarter revenue to rise about 12%, driven by subscriber growth, selective price hikes and expanding advertising revenue. Netflix also narrowed its 2026 revenue guidance to $51 billion to $51.4 billion. Meanwhile, veteran investor Michael Burry said last week that he is on the fence about whether Netflix produces content “that is long-lasting, watchable on repeat, across generations.” Drawing comparisons with peers Disney and Pixar, he said the rivals “produce evergreen content,” raising questions about whether Netflix’s content can generate similar long-term value. NFLX stock is down more than 24% this year even as retail sentiment remains ‘extremely bullish’ on Stocktwits. ORCL stock fell to a 52-week low of $121.50 on Friday, although the company’s shares recovered to close in the green. Oracle has been on the receiving end of criticism for its aggressive spending on cloud infrastructure and rapidly growing debt. The company recently said that it plans to spend up to $95 billion in capital expenditures in fiscal 2027 and raise $40 billion through debt and equity. This has fueled worries about rising leverage and negative free cash flow. Those concerns intensified after S&P Global downgraded Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, citing its reliance on a handful of large customers, including OpenAI. The company has also been weighed down by growing uncertainty around OpenAI's business prospects, raising questions about Oracle's AI-driven growth strategy. ORCL stock is down more than 35% this year. Despite the worries, retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘extremely bullish’ at the time of writing as users see the dip as an opportunity. SPCX stock fell to an all-time low of $122.12, dipping further below its IPO price of $135. Elon Musk’s aerospace company, which made its historic debut on Wall Street last month, declined for a sixth-straight session. SpaceX has seen heavy selling following its aggressive capital-raising plans. Meanwhile, last week the company scrubbed the latest launch of its Starship mega rocket due to technical glitches. Musk said in a post on X that the launch was automatically aborted after some of the engines failed to ignite. In a separate post, he said SpaceX plans to replace two Raptor engines before making another launch attempt, which is most likely to take place early next week. The test flight was intended to mark the debut of an upgraded version of Starship designed to support future Starlink deployments and NASA's lunar missions. According to a Reuters report, SpaceX is now targeting July 23 for its next launch attempt. Shares of Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) jumped 3% overnight late Monday as retail traders bet that the final acute myeloid leukemia (AML) readout could turn this week’s Fox appearance into a launchpad for Big Pharma interest. SLS stock surged 12% on Friday to close at $13.19, capping a 3% weekly gain. The speculation is related to Sellas’ Phase 3 Regal trial of galinpepimut-S (GPS) in AML. The study is nearing the 80th event required to trigger its final analysis. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits sllipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a week ago amid a 12% rise in 24-hour message volumes. However, watchers for the stock have risen nearly 5% in a month. One trader called CEO Angelos Stergiou’s media strategy a “masterclass in forcing a Big Pharma decision,” saying that the period between the 80th event and topline data could trap short sellers. “We aren't waiting for a buyout—we’re manufacturing the conditions that make a bidding war inevitable,” the user said. Another investor expects Sellas to announce the topline results around Stergiou’s Fox appearance, while projecting a surge in the stock and a bidding war.  A third user said Stergiou had spent more than five years protecting Regal and would not risk the program for “30 minutes of television fame,” adding: “The timeline is compressed because the destination is set.” Other traders predicted that Stergiou would discuss the company’s two flagship drugs and the path to topline data. Several named Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Pfizer, AbbVie, Eli Lilly, and Bristol Myers as possible bidders. “One thing is for sure, JnJ will be watching Fox News,” another user said, citing LinkedIn activity. Stergiou said on LinkedIn last week that he would return to Fox & Friends after a recent discussion with host Brian Kilmeade about the future of AI-powered cancer vaccines. He said that the segment’s date and time were still being finalized, adding that the discussion would cover Sellas’ clinical programs and efforts to advance more personalized cancer care through GPS and SLS009 (the company’s second clinical-stage drug candidate). Meanwhile, retail takeover speculation has intensified as the market value swelled from about $73 million at the start of 2024 to more than $1.5 billion by mid-2026, with Regal nearing completion. Investors have pointed to Stergiou’s previous references to “strategic partners,” changes to executive change-of-control benefits and the potential commercial value of GPS and SLS009 (the second drug). Regal is a Phase 3 study evaluating GPS in AML patients who have entered a second complete remission. The trial had reached 78 of the 80 events required to trigger its final analysis. Sellas has said that the study would be considered successful if GPS extends median overall survival to 12.6 months, compared with eight months for best available therapy. Stergiou previously said the company would announce the 80th event and then enter a formal quiet period until topline results are available. He has also pushed back against claims that the slower event rate necessarily means patients in the control arm are surviving longer. Since Sellas remains blinded, neither the company nor investors know which arm is responsible for the slower accumulation of events. The CEO has also rejected calls to stop the trial at 78 events, saying, “Events are our statistical currency,” and warning that an early halt could create regulatory concerns and timing bias. Investors are weighing stronger oil-market conditions against valuation risks and the possibility that a reversal in crude prices could limit further gains. Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM) shares climbed to a 52-week high as geopolitical tensions and concerns over global oil supplies supported energy stocks. The rally has strengthened the outlook for the U.S. oil major, but investors face a critical question: how much upside remains after the recent advance? With crude prices volatile and the company’s next earnings report approaching, Exxon Mobil stock is now at a crucial point, raising the question of whether XOM stock price can extend its rally or if investors should expect a pullback. Exxon Mobil shares rose 1.68% to close at $177.01 on October 14, after reaching an intraday high of $177.43. The move extended the stock’s gains for a fifth consecutive session, reflecting renewed buying interest in the energy sector. Higher crude prices and concerns about supply disruptions have supported energy stocks. Recent attacks affecting Middle Eastern energy infrastructure and shipping routes have increased uncertainty over global oil flows, strengthening the market’s focus on producers with large-scale operations and established cash-generation capacity. Exxon has also received support from improving earnings expectations. Zacks upgraded the stock to a Buy rating, while analyst estimates for the company’s 2026 earnings have increased. However, the broader analyst consensus remains more cautious, highlighting the risk that the share price has advanced ahead of expectations for future earnings. Oil prices remain a key driver of Exxon’s financial performance. Higher crude prices can improve upstream earnings and cash generation, although refining margins, commodity-price movements and operating costs also influence overall results. Investors will be watching whether the current supply risks translate into sustained higher prices or whether crude retreats as market conditions change. A prolonged period of elevated prices could support Exxon’s earnings outlook, while a sharp reversal could reduce the financial benefits of the recent rally. The company’s next quarterly results will provide a clearer view of how commodity prices and operating performance are affecting profitability. Exxon is scheduled to report its third-quarter 2026 results on October 30, according to the current earnings calendar. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is set to rule on five closely watched treatments in August from Moderna, Lantheus Holdings, Bristol Myers Squibb, Capricor Therapeutics and Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical. Decisions are due by August 23 at the latest on therapies ranging from an mRNA flu vaccine to a gene therapy for a rare metabolic disorder, putting biotech investors on high alert as the outcomes could drive sharp near-term moves across the sector. Moderna is seeking approval for mRNA-1010, its experimental mRNA-based seasonal flu vaccine for adults 50 and older. An FDA advisory panel already voted unanimously in favor of the shot in June, and the FDA is slated to decide on its application by August 5. The FDA initially refused to file Moderna’s application in early February 2026, citing concerns that the comparator vaccine used in the main trial did not reflect the best available care for older adults. Moderna revised its plan, and now the company is seeking a traditional approval for adults aged 50-64 and an accelerated approval for adults 65 and older. If granted accelerated approval in the patient population, Moderna will be required to conduct another study to confirm effectiveness in the group. Lantheus wants approval for MK-6240, a PET imaging agent that detects tau protein tangles in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. Doctors would use the scan to help confirm the presence of tau pathology, stage the disease, and guide treatment decisions. The FDA accepted the company’s application seeking approval in October and granted it a fast-track designation. The application is based on two late-stage trials in people with early Alzheimer’s disease. In both trials, the scan identified patients with tau pathology and ruled out people without it, to support the application. The FDA will decide on the application by August 13 at the latest. Bristol Myers Squibb is seeking approval for iberdomide, an oral drug combined with existing medicines for patients whose multiple myeloma has returned or stopped responding, by August 17. It works by helping the immune system attack cancer cells more effectively while also directly killing myeloma cells. Bristol Myers’ application was accepted by the FDA in February and granted priority review. The application relies on the large late-stage trial where iberdomide, together with Daratumumab and Dexamethasone, showed a statistically significant improvement in minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity rates compared to control arms. MRD negativity means no detectable cancer cells remain after treatment — an early sign of deep response. Capricor is seeking full approval for Deramiocel, a cell therapy aimed at heart damage caused by Duchenne muscular dystrophy. After an earlier rejection, the company submitted new data from its late-stage HOPE-3 trial to the FDA. However, in July, an advisory committee voted 9–3 against the claim that the available evidence provides substantial proof of effectiveness for treating DMD cardiomyopathy. The vote is non-binding, meaning the FDA could still approve the therapy. Ultragenyx is seeking approval for DTX401, a one-time gene therapy for glycogen storage disease type Ia, a rare inherited metabolic disorder, by August 23. People with GSDIa cannot release stored sugar from the liver, leading to dangerous drops in blood sugar (hypoglycemia) during fasting, excess glycogen buildup in the liver and kidneys, and other long-term complications. The FDA granted priority review to Ultragenyx’s application in February. There are currently no approved treatments that address the underlying cause of GSDIa. content: At 22.2 times earnings, ExxonMobil (XOM) stock trades near the S&P 500’s 22.5. Shareholders paying that multiple need a clear view of the underlying assets, and the priorities inside the company have shifted. During the fiscal Q3 2024 call, executives promoted Pioneer Natural Resources, a producer ExxonMobil now owns outright. Management no longer emphasizes that deal. So what does management talk up instead? During the fiscal Q2 2026 call in July, management pointed to Guyana as one of the clearest examples of growth. Executives also made the case for Energy Products. This refining and fuels business set a record for second-quarter diesel production. Management also pointed to record Permian production of more than 1.8 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, the basin where the Pioneer barrels sit, though it no longer credits the deal by name. In their fiscal 2024 calls, executives had focused on the barrels ExxonMobil had purchased. Management noted on the fiscal Q3 2024 call that Pioneer added 770,000 oil-equivalent barrels per day. By the fiscal Q4 2024 call, the company was still outlining synergies from the combined assets. If you have held ExxonMobil for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not what management says next. See how a tax-aware transition works. ExxonMobil’s Fuel Sales Far Outstrip Its Oilfield Revenue Energy Products brought in $290.3 billion in fiscal 2025. That figure was down 6.5% from fiscal 2024. Upstream, the oil and gas production business, brought in $101.8 billion, down 1.7%. Neither division grew its revenue in fiscal 2025. Still, before internal sales between divisions are netted out, Energy Products sells close to three times as much as Upstream, and it is one of the areas management now highlights. Measured by earnings, however, Energy Products represents a smaller piece of ExxonMobil. It accounts for about 23% of business line earnings, which management noted is up from about 9% five years ago. When addressing growth, management points to Guyana. The region delivered gross production of about 900,000 barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026. Shareholders cannot rely on those margins with confidence. That reality makes the recent change in emphasis more concerning than reassuring for a holder. Management noted in July that disruption shaped the second quarter. With a major shipping route closed, roughly 3 million barrels a day of refining capacity was cut off from the market. The fuel margins management currently highlights appear to come partly from that missing supply. Policy presents a second risk to those margins. Windfall taxes came up in July through a question noting that one European country had approved them on the downstream. Management said ExxonMobil canceled investments it had planned for Europe the last time such a tax passed there. Guyana represents the other part of the new emphasis. Management indicated that ExxonMobil recovered its capital and cost there nearly two years earlier than anticipated. title: These 3 Oil Giants Make Money Beyond the Wellhead. That’s Good News for Dividends - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Oil prices crashed 14% last year, yet three energy giants kept raising their dividends anyway. The integrated business model behind that trick also explains why analysts see one of them as the most recession-proof income stock in the sector. Oil prices swing hard, and retirement budgets can’t. Integrated majors close that gap by owning the whole chain. When crude falls, cheaper feedstock tends to widen refining and chemicals margins, so one division supports another and the dividend keeps coming. TotalEnergies (NYSE:TTE | TTE Price Prediction) showed how this works in fiscal 2025, when its Refining and Chemicals segment grew adjusted net operating income 10% in a year when Brent crude fell 14%. TotalEnergies, Chevron (NYSE:CVX) and Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM) all run upstream, downstream and chemicals operations under one roof. All three are raising their payouts, and all three pay those dividends out of operating cash flow. Chevron yields 2.98% on a quarterly dividend of $1.78, or $7.12 a year. The yield looks modest because the stock has climbed 47.85% year to date to $219.25. The dividend itself keeps growing. Track record: This year’s 4% raise was Chevron’s 39th consecutive annual increase, according to the company. The payment record supports the recent run. Over the past five years, the quarterly rate has gone from $1.42 to $1.51, $1.63, $1.71 and now $1.78. Coverage and balance sheet: Chevron’s free cash flow yield of 3.88% is about 1.3 times its dividend yield. Second-quarter 2026 free cash flow reached $18.10 billion on operating cash flow of $22.63 billion. That one quarter beat the $16.6 billion of free cash flow Chevron produced in all of 2025. Debt is low: debt-to-equity is 0.219, net debt to EBITDA is 0.94 and interest coverage is 13.7x. Chevron also paid down $8.41 billion of debt in the quarter. In 2025 it returned $27.1 billion to shareholders. For the bull case,  the Hess acquisition gave Chevron a interest in Guyana’s Stabroek block. Worldwide production rose 20% year over year to 4,070 MBOED, and U.S. upstream output hit a record 2,077 MBOED. The integrated model paid off as well: downstream earnings reached $4.87 billion, up from $737 million a year earlier. Chevron reached $3 billion in run-rate structural cost cuts six months ahead of schedule and captured $1.5 billion in Hess synergies within a year of closing. It also signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) for a 2.67 GW West Texas data center, which adds long-term revenue tied to AI power demand. Risk: Measured against reported earnings, the payout is stretched. The $7.12 annualized dividend is higher than Chevron’s 2025 EPS of $6.63, and a P/E near 35 shows earnings still trailing the share price. Today’s cash flow covers the dividend easily, but a long slump in oil would reduce that supports quickly. Exxon Mobil yields 2.41% on a $1.03 quarterly dividend, or $4.12 a year. As with Chevron, a strong rally has pushed the yield down: shares are up 48.12% year to date at $174.77. Track record: Exxon reports 43 consecutive years of annual dividend-per-share growth. The company’s most recent increase was 4%, in the fourth quarter of 2025. The quarterly rate has climbed from $0.41 in 1999 to $1.03 today. Recent increases were $0.88, $0.91, $0.95, $0.99 and $1.03. Coverage and balance sheet: The forward dividend works out to about 61% of 2025 EPS of $6.70. The 3.30% free cash flow yield is about 1.4 times the dividend yield. It has the strongest balance sheet of the three, with debt-to-equity of 0.168, net debt to EBITDA of 0.548 and interest coverage running at 56.3x. Bull case: Exxon’s growth comes from low-cost barrels. Advantaged assets (the Permian, Guyana and LNG) made up 59% of 2025 production. Upstream output hit a record 4.7 million boe per day, the highest in more than 40 years, and Guyana now tops 900,000 gross barrels a day. All 10 of 10 key 2025 projects started up, and Golden Pass LNG has loaded its first export cargo. Total structural cost savings of $15.6 billion since 2019 are heading toward a $20 billion target by 2030. Lower costs let Exxon keep paying the dividend at lower oil prices. Risk: Quarterly results can swing sharply. First-quarter 2026 reported net income was $4.18 billion after a $3.88 billion hit from derivative timing and $706 million of losses from Middle East supply disruptions. Free cash flow was only $2.70 billion, while buybacks totaled $4.9 billion. Exxon has also committed to $20 billion of buybacks and $27 billion to $29 billion of capex this year. If weak quarters pile up, the buyback is the spending Exxon can most easily cut. TotalEnergies is the high-yield name of the group at 4.56%. Its next payment is $1.021 per share, and its annualized forward dividend is $4.084. Track record: The board raised the fiscal 2025 dividend 5.6% to €3.40 per share. It then set the first 2026 interim payment at €0.90, up 5.9%. The available payment record goes back to 2007. Coverage and balance sheet: Trailing dividends of $4.052 per share equal about 51% of trailing EPS of $7.99, the most conservative earnings payout of the three. In 2025, operating cash flow of $27.343 billion easily covered $16.953 billion of capex and still left room for $7.5 billion in buybacks. Management’s plan calls for cash flow above $26 billion with Brent at $60, and gearing targeted around 15% at year-end. The stock trades at about 11 times trailing earnings and 9 times forward estimates. Chevron trades near 35 times trailing earnings and Exxon near 25. Bull case: TotalEnergies runs the most diverse business of the three. It sold 43.9 Mt of LNG and produced 48.1 TWh of net electricity, while hydrocarbon production grew 4% to 2,529 kboe/d. In the full-year results, chief executive Patrick Pouyanné said the company “reaped the benefits of its integrated and balanced multi-energy strategy” in a year of falling oil prices. A $12.5 billion cash-savings plan running through 2030 gives the dividend another layer of support. Risk: TotalEnergies sets its dividend in euros, so the dollar amount U.S. holders receive moves with exchange rates. The latest payment of $1.021 followed one of $0.969365. A stronger dollar can reduce the check even in a year when the euro dividend goes up. Every dividend on this list depends on oil and gas prices that these companies don’t control. Much of the recent jump in cash flow came from Brent at $104 a barrel, compared with $68 a year earlier. Part of that rise came from Middle East disruptions, which also shut in about 15% of TotalEnergies’ production at one point. Prices that spike during a conflict can fall just as fast once supply returns or OPEC+ changes its quotas. The energy transition is the slower threat. Electrification and climate policy will weigh on long-term oil demand, and TotalEnergies already faces climate litigation in France, Belgium and the United States. Integration, low-cost barrels and cost cuts make these companies more resilient, but they still sell hydrocarbons. In a $60 oil world, retirees should expect slower dividend growth, and that is the price TotalEnergies plans its budget around. Exxon Mobil has the most protected payout of the trio, with a 43-year growth run and the cleanest balance sheet. Chevron pairs 39 straight raises with free cash flow that well tops its dividend. TotalEnergies pays the most income per dollar invested at the lowest valuation, with currency swings as the trade-off. Together, they show how the integrated model is designed to support dividends across oil cycles, with each segment cushioning the others when prices move. An exchange that helped define modern crypto derivatives is closing its doors soon. BitMEX, the crypto derivatives exchange co-founded by Arthur Hayes in 2014 that introduced perpetual swaps and 100x leverage trading, will cease operations in September, following a strategic review by its owner, HDR Global Trading Limited. The news sent BitMEX's native token, BMEX, plunging over 90% on Thursday. This move comes at a time when decentralized perpetual exchanges led by Hyperliquid (HYPE) continue to chip away at centralized rivals’ market share. The exchange announced that it will shut down on September 23¯. The company framed the closure as an end of a chapter rather than a distressed exit, saying in its statement that“It may not look the same today, but we are proud of our 11+ year legacy and the role we played in shaping the crypto industry. Registration for new users is no longer being accepted. Starting August 26, users will only be able to reduce existing positions, not take new trades. Any positions not closed by the September 23 deadline will be forcibly liquidated. BitMEX said user assets remained fully secure and under customer control during the wind-down, but know-your-customer (KYC)- verified users who do not withdraw in time will be charged an account management fee. In 2022, BitMEX and its three co-founders, Hayes, Ben Delo, and Samuel Reed, pleaded guilty to violations of the Bank Secrecy Act for failing to maintain an anti-money laundering (AML) program, paying a combined $30 million in Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) penalties. President Trump pardoned all three founders in March 2025, wiping away their convictions just about a year before the exchange’s own shutdown announcement. BitMEX’s shutdown also comes amidst a broader market-structure shift. Benchmarks have moved in choppy fashion, with worries about ample supply bumping against bouts of firmer demand and geopolitical headlines. For an oil major of this size, those swings feed directly into the revenue the upstream arm pulls from each barrel it lifts, so the commodity tape tends to drive much of the day-to-day mood around the stock. Softer crude can squeeze the margins the company earns on production, yet the integrated model offers a cushion. At the heart of the business sits a vast upstream arm that pumps crude and natural gas from fields spread across the Americas, Africa and beyond. The company has poured capital into high-quality acreage, with a heavy tilt toward the Permian Basin in the American Southwest and offshore developments that have become showpieces of its growth plans. These barrels tend to carry low operating costs, which helps the group stay resilient even when crude drifts lower. Management has framed the growth story around lifting output from these advantaged assets while keeping spending disciplined. The chemicals arm, in particular, ties the company to the broader industrial economy. Demand for packaging, construction materials and consumer goods flows through these product lines, so the segment can lean on trends that sit apart from the energy cycle. Geography adds further balance to the downstream arm. That spread helps keep the segment humming even when any given economy wobbles. Readers following Oil and Gas Stocks can place this update within its wider category. Natural gas forms another pillar of the operating story. The company controls a large gas resource base and has expanded its reach into liquefied natural gas, shipping the fuel to markets across Europe and Asia where demand for cleaner-burning energy has grown. As power grids lean on gas to balance the swing toward renewables, this part of the portfolio ties the group to a durable thread of global demand. The push into liquefied natural gas has placed the company alongside a handful of global players shaping how the fuel moves across oceans. Zooming out, the broader group of US Oil and Gas Stocks has been navigating a backdrop defined by swinging prices, shifting supply decisions from OPEC+ and a steady drumbeat of talk about the energy transition. American producers have leaned on capital discipline, keeping spending in check rather than flooding the market with new barrels, and that restraint has shaped how the whole complex trades through choppy stretches. Within that landscape, the largest integrated majors tend to attract the most attention because of their scale and their ability to keep operating through downturns that strain smaller rivals. The company sits squarely in that top tier, and its moves are often read as a signal for how the entire American energy space is faring at any given moment. A central force hanging over the whole sector has been the stance of OPEC+ on supply. The group of major exporting nations has been managing how much crude flows onto the market, and each adjustment sends waves through global benchmarks. When the alliance signals more barrels, prices often soften; when it pulls back, the market can firm. That tug-of-war has kept crude in a choppy range through much of the current year. A recurring theme across the majors has been restraint on spending. Rather than racing to expand at the initial sign of firmer prices, the company has emphasized disciplined capital allocation, steering money toward its lowest-cost barrels and its highest-value projects. That approach is meant to keep the business durable through the inevitable troughs of the commodity cycle. Alongside spending restraint, the group has leaned on a steady cadence of dividends and cash distribution that has long drawn a dedicated base of market participants.
